title: fix(status): include validated release SHA in readiness
body:
## Summary

```text
Argus cached /api/ready
  status + ready + reason_codes
  + source_sha only when build revision is a validated 40-character SHA
```

This gives Janitor a bounded release identity on its existing read-only observation. Detailed admin status remains separate.

## Evidence

- **Before:** Janitor's Argus operation received HTTP 200 but recorded `response_sha_missing`.
- **After:** Valid build revisions appear as `source_sha`; unknown revisions omit the field. Focused operational status tests: 84 passed. Ruff and `git diff --check` pass.
- **Runtime gate:** This is source only. Exact image promotion and a later natural Janitor receipt are required before #296 can count Argus identity as verified.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** two-way

**Blast Radius:** public cached readiness response

The new field is validated release metadata; it does not run a dependency probe or expose admin status.

title: Keep fork PR reviews off private OCI runner
body:
## Summary

```diff

+require same-repository head

```

Require the PR head repository to match Argus before either review job reaches the self-hosted runner. Issue triage is unchanged. Supports Homelab [#296](https://github.com/Khamel83/homelab/issues/296).

## Evidence

- **Before:** `fast-review` and `deep-review` accepted any `pull_request` event, including a public fork.

## Merge Danger

**Blast Radius:** review

Fork PRs will no longer receive the private fast or deep review. Same-repository PRs keep those jobs.

title: AI chat share links extract only 'Sign in' (Gemini, ChatGPT)
body:
Public AI chat share links return only site chrome from Argus extraction.

Observed 2026-09-25: `extract_content_v2` on `https://share.gemini.google/bQBdWIDX3xBr` → `extraction_failed`, 2 words ("Sign in"), extractor trafilatura, machine homelab. The conversation is rendered client-side.

Headless Chrome (Playwright, `wait_until=networkidle` + ~4 s) on the Mac mini reads the full conversation for:
- Gemini: `share.gemini.google/<id>` (redirects to `gemini.google.com/share/<id>`)
- ChatGPT: `chatgpt.com/share/<id>`

Claude `claude.ai/share/<id>` is not yet verified against a real public share (an invalid id redirects to `/login`).

Working reference: `~/.claude/skills/read-share-link/read_share.py` on the Mac mini (renders, strips site chrome, exits 2 on a login wall).

## Acceptance
- The chain reaches its Playwright stage for these hosts instead of accepting/failing on the trafilatura result; the cross-domain redirect `share.gemini.google → gemini.google.com` is admitted by browser policy.
- Site chrome (navigation, "Sign in", footer) is removed; a login redirect is reported as not public, never as content.
- Canary tests for one Gemini and one ChatGPT public share.

title: Document scorecard admission operations and Homelab coordination
body:
Parent issue: #151

## What
Document the scorecard concurrency limit, capacity thresholds, queue and backoff behavior, recovery semantics, rollback controls, and coordination with Homelab runner-demand scheduling. Include the qualification procedure and operator signals needed to distinguish queued work from a failed workload.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Documentation names every admission and pressure setting, its default, its valid range, and its operational effect.
- [ ] Documentation explains that baseline and candidate jobs consume one shared host budget and that no Docker resources are created before admission.
- [ ] Queue states, retry/backoff behavior, cancellation, lease expiry, and worker-crash recovery are described.
- [ ] A rollback or emergency-disable procedure is documented and can be applied without deleting unrelated scorecard or Homelab data.
- [ ] Coordination with Homelab runner-demand scheduling is explicit, including how scorecard admission avoids competing with five-second evidence checks.
- [ ] The bounded qualification command, expected pass criteria, and evidence artifacts are documented.

title: Add a bounded scorecard qualification run for Baywatch evidence latency
body:
Parent issue: #151

## What
Create a repeatable qualification command or harness that runs bounded baseline and candidate scorecard activity while exercising the local Baywatch evidence calls used for Docker, Hermes, and Homelab runner-demand checks. Record admission, queue, resource-pressure, and evidence-call timing so the protection can be evaluated without using a production database or deployment.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The qualification run starts bounded baseline and candidate activity through the real scorecard execution path.
- [ ] The run exercises the local Baywatch evidence calls concurrently with scorecard activity, including Docker, Hermes, and Homelab runner-demand checks.
- [ ] Every evidence call has a five-second deadline, and the run fails if any call exceeds that deadline or fails closed unexpectedly.
- [ ] The run reports the maximum evidence latency, active scorecard count, queue transitions, and Docker object/interface pressure before, during, and after execution.
- [ ] The run leaves no scorecard containers, networks, leases, or queue entries behind after completion or interruption.
- [ ] The qualification procedure is safe for a disposable local environment and does not target production databases or deployments.

title: Queue and safely recover scorecard workloads denied by admission
body:
Parent issue: #151

## What
Integrate queueing and bounded backoff into scorecard execution so capacity denial delays the complete workload instead of partially starting it. Add cancellation, retry limits, lease cleanup, and recovery for abandoned queue entries or expired admissions.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A capacity-denied baseline or candidate request enters a bounded queue and does not initialize Docker resources while waiting.
- [ ] Retries use bounded exponential backoff with a maximum wait or retry policy and do not busy-loop.
- [ ] Queue status distinguishes waiting, admitted, canceled, failed, and completed work without exposing host details.
- [ ] Cancellation removes waiting work and releases any acquired admission before returning.
- [ ] Startup failures and worker termination release leases and allow later queued work to proceed.
- [ ] A test exercises two concurrent jobs, verifies that the second waits, and verifies that it starts only after the first releases admission.

title: Gate scorecard admission on bounded host and Docker pressure
body:
Parent issue: #151

## What
Add capacity probes and an admission policy for the scorecard coordinator. Evaluate bounded host capacity before workload startup using CPU, available memory, Docker object/interface pressure, and the number of active scorecard jobs. Keep thresholds configurable with safe defaults and make probe failures fail closed to queueing rather than allowing an unbounded workload.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Admission evaluates CPU capacity, available memory, Docker container/network pressure, interface or veth pressure, and active scorecard jobs before startup.
- [ ] Each metric has a bounded threshold or budget with a documented default and validated configuration.
- [ ] A workload is not admitted when any required capacity check is unavailable or over threshold.
- [ ] Capacity is rechecked after waiting and immediately before Docker workload creation.
- [ ] Tests cover each pressure boundary and verify that a rejected admission creates no container, network, or exec resource.
- [ ] The policy returns a stable, content-free reason code suitable for logs and queue state.

title: Add a host-wide shared admission budget for Argus scorecard jobs
body:
Parent issue: #151

## What
Implement a host-wide scorecard admission coordinator used by both baseline and candidate execution paths. The coordinator must enforce one shared active-job budget rather than separate limits per execution mode. Use a bounded default of one active scorecard workload, with an explicit configuration override and an atomic acquire/release or lease mechanism that recovers when a worker exits unexpectedly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Baseline and candidate jobs acquire the same host-scoped admission budget before creating any Docker container, network, or exec stream.
- [ ] The default active scorecard workload limit is one and the configured limit is validated as a bounded positive value.
- [ ] Concurrent baseline and candidate launches cannot exceed the shared limit, including when they start from separate worker processes.
- [ ] Admission state is released on success, failure, cancellation, and worker termination recovery.
- [ ] Tests demonstrate that a second job cannot enter workload startup while the first job holds the shared admission.
- [ ] The admission result exposes stable states for admitted, queued, and unavailable without leaking host-specific diagnostics.

title: Bound scorecard concurrency to protect Docker and network health evidence
body:
## Context

During the 2026-09-14 05:34–05:39 UTC window, Argus scorecard baseline/candidate jobs created a burst of Docker containers and networks while Homelab runner-demand checks were active.

Observed host evidence included:

- repeated Docker network and veth creation;
- canceled /containers/json?all=1 requests and Docker broken-pipe responses;
- closed exec streams and stopped-container health probes;
- repeated host No buffer space available interface errors;
- Baywatch delegated evidence calls failing closed for baywatch.timer, Hermes, and Homelab together.

The Docker daemon did not restart and no OOM event was found in the inspected window, but the control plane was sufficiently pressured to starve five-second health evidence calls.

## Goal

Bound Argus scorecard ephemeral workload concurrency so scorecard execution cannot degrade the Homelab Docker/network control plane or monitoring evidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- Argus scorecard baseline/candidate execution has an explicit host concurrency limit or queue.
- Concurrent baseline/candidate runs share one admission budget and cannot independently multiply container/network pressure.
- Admission considers bounded host capacity such as CPU, memory, Docker object/interface pressure, and active scorecard jobs.
- When capacity is unavailable, work queues or backs off with a content-free reason and does not partially start a workload.
- A bounded qualification run demonstrates that Baywatch local evidence calls remain within their five-second budget while scorecard activity runs.
- The limit, queue behavior, and recovery/rollback path are documented.
- Any required coordination with Homelab runner-demand scheduling is explicitly documented.

## Notes

This is an infrastructure follow-up to the transient Baywatch incident documented in https://github.com/Khamel83/homelab/blob/main/docs/HANDOFF.md; it is not evidence that Hermes itself crashed.

title: feat: add scoped paywall browser exception (#148)
body:
## Summary
Option 1 from #148. Paywalled extraction (NYT, WSJ, and other cookie-backed domains) has failed with `browser_policy_unavailable` since `07b807e`, because no browser-network attestation provider exists. This adds a scoped, **off-by-default** exception.

- New `ARGUS_AUTH_BROWSER_DOMAINS` (comma-separated). A browser request is admitted without an attestation only when **all** of these hold:
  - profile is `authenticated_content`
  - the URL is HTTPS
  - the host (or a parent) is on the allowlist
  - the host is in `PAYWALL_DOMAINS`
  - a cookie file exists for it
- It applies **only when no attestation is present**. An installed authority that returns an invalid or expired attestation still wins.
- **Receipt:** `BrowserAdmission.basis == "auth_browser_exception"` and `exception_ref == "ARGUS_AUTH_BROWSER_DOMAINS:<domain>"`, with `attestation=None` and a 5-minute lease. Each such admission logs a warning.
- The existing same-origin resource guard for `authenticated_content` is unchanged.
- Both gates on the auth path (`guarded.open_browser_session` and `admit_browser_url`) go through `require_browser_policy`, so a single hook covers both.
- `ARGUS_AUTH_BROWSER_DOMAINS` joins the authority-only inputs that the MCP adapter rejects.
- Readiness is unchanged. No attestation provider is installed, so browser attestation still reads as missing.
- Docs: README env table, `.env.example`, CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]`.

Remove this once option 2, the real browser-network authority, lands.

## Known pre-existing limit (not changed here)
`auth_extractor` caches one browser context per domain. That context's route guard stays bound to the **first** admission: its origin and its `max_resources` counter. Across many articles on one domain, later pages can hit "browser resource limit exceeded", or have a different subdomain blocked as cross-origin. That needs a follow-up if it shows up in production.

## Test plan
- [x] 12 new tests: off by default; admits an allowlisted, cookie-backed paywall host with a receipt; rejects missing cookies, non-paywall hosts, hosts not on the allowlist, plain HTTP, lookalike hosts, and `public_content`; never overrides a rejecting authority; keeps the same-origin guard through `admit_browser_url`; MCP adapter rejects the variable.
- [x] Full suite: 2932 passed, 47 skipped
- [x] `ruff check`, `scripts/verify_release_contract.py`, hermetic scorecard (`stable`)
- [ ] Live: with the switch on, one NYT and one WSJ article extract from homelab; with it off, both fail closed

title: Paywall login browser: scoped exception now, browser-network attestation long-term
body:
## Problem

Atlas saves paywalled articles (NYT, WSJ, Bloomberg, LA Times, Chicago Tribune, ESPN, Stratechery) through Argus. Since `07b807e` (2026-09-02, "gate browser acquisition on connection policy"), every browser admission fails closed: `UnavailableBrowserAttestationProvider` is the only provider, and nothing installs another. So `extract_authenticated` returns `auth: browser_policy_unavailable` even when the cookies are valid. TODO.md already says: "Admit a real external browser-network authority/attestation … Keep browser access fail-closed meanwhile."

### Evidence, 2026-09-14, homelab
- The cookies are now at `/data/cookies` (`ARGUS_COOKIE_DIR`), owner `argus`, mode 600. For nytimes.com, `needs_auth`, `get_cookie_path` and `can_authenticate` are all true.
- `extract_authenticated(nyt_url)` returns `auth: browser_policy_unavailable`.
- Plain HTTP with the same cookies gets NYT 403 and WSJ 401. Bot protection blocks non-browser clients, so a browser is required.
- The browser used to work: sandboxed Chromium shipped in `f84565f` (2026-07-23), and the bounded raw browser fetch in `4ba0ede` (2026-07-29).

## Plan

### 1. Now: a scoped, switchable exception
- A setting that is off by default, for example `ARGUS_AUTH_BROWSER_DOMAINS`. It admits the browser only for the `authenticated_content` profile, only for cookie-backed domains in `PAYWALL_DOMAINS` that are also on that allowlist, and only for same-origin navigation. That is the existing `authenticated_content` same-origin rule.
- Every admission still records a receipt that it went through the exception, not through an attestation. Readiness keeps reporting browser attestation as missing.
- Everything else (raw browser fetch, generic Playwright, Obscura, residential) stays fail-closed.

### 2. Long-term: the real browser-network authority
- An isolated browser network with enforced egress, and an attestation provider that `validate_browser_attestation` accepts: policy identity, resolver/address-control identity, connection binding, release identity, and expiry.
- Once it is in place, retire the exception in item 1.

## Alternatives already on file
- #142 Obscura (anti-detection CDP browser) and #139 CloakBrowser (fingerprint-patched Chromium). Both target the bot protection behind the NYT and WSJ 403/401s.
- #143 Lightpanda, #140 Scrapling, #144 crawl4ai: lighter or stealthier browser runtimes.
- #141 Firecrawl: a paid API. It cannot use the user's subscriptions, so it doesn't help with paywalls.
- The archive fallbacks (Wayback, archive.is) are **not** an option for Maya-origin saves: Atlas's deny-archive policy (`7c4fb139`, 2026-08-09).
- Cookie freshness: the files were exported 2026-04-05. NYT has 3 of 6 cookies still valid. Re-export from a logged-in browser when auth starts failing. The old auto-login service (`argus-extract-service`, retired in May) could come back as a cookie refresher.

## Done means
- [ ] With the switch on, one NYT and one WSJ article extract through the auth browser from homelab. With it off, both fail closed.
- [ ] Tests cover off-by-default, the allowlist, same-origin navigation, and the receipt marking.
- [ ] Item 2 is tracked to completion, and the exception is removed after it lands.

Related: Khamel83/atlas#32, Khamel83/homelab#243.

**Capability:** Run standard OCI-compatible Linux container images as lightweight virtual machines on Apple-silicon Macs using Apple’s native `container` CLI.

- **Repository:** [apple/container](https://github.com/apple/container)
- **Description:** A tool for creating and running Linux containers using lightweight virtual machines on a Mac. It is written in Swift, and optimized for Apple silicon. 
- **Latest observed commit:** 8ca5c80c380cdd925d87b497fb23eddb6b58843f

- **Recent commits in window:** 165
- **Target subsystem:** `Argus standalone/development container deployment defined by `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`, including the published `ghcr.io/khamel83/argus` image.`

## Direct relationship

Add an optional macOS 26 Apple-silicon development launcher that runs Argus’s existing OCI image through `container`, mapping the current port, environment, and persistent `/var/lib/argus` storage configuration without changing the canonical Docker Compose or homelab deployment paths.

Supporting evidence:
- The source explicitly consumes and produces OCI-compatible images and can pull and run images from standard container registries.
- The target has a `Dockerfile`, a Docker Compose service, and a README badge identifying the published `ghcr.io/khamel83/argus` container image.
- The target container exposes Argus on port 8000 and defines a concrete runtime contract through environment variables and `/var/lib/argus` persistence in `docker-compose.yml`.
- The source is optimized for Apple silicon and requires macOS 26, matching a concrete local-development environment rather than suggesting a generic production-runtime replacement.
- The source is active, unarchived, and reached v1.0.0 in the supplied recent commits.

## Expected benefit

Apple-silicon contributors on macOS 26 could run Argus’s existing Linux image without Docker Desktop while retaining OCI portability and isolating Playwright and extraction dependencies inside a lightweight VM.

## Proposed implementation outline

1. Keep `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` as the canonical portable definitions.
1. Create an optional macOS launcher that checks for Apple silicon, macOS 26, and an available `container` system service.
1. Run the published Argus OCI image, or an image built from the existing Dockerfile, with port 8000 exposed and the existing `ARGUS_*` environment contract applied.
1. Attach persistent storage for `/var/lib/argus` and reproduce read-only filesystem, temporary storage, and resource restrictions only where the `container` CLI demonstrably supports equivalent controls.
1. Exercise `/api/live`, SQLite persistence across restarts, and a Playwright-backed extraction path before documenting the launcher as supported.

## Compatibility and risks

Strong at the image boundary because both projects explicitly use standard OCI images. The integration should remain an optional local macOS path: the supplied evidence does not establish Docker Compose compatibility or equivalents for every Compose security, healthcheck, tmpfs, volume, and resource-control option.

- Only Apple-silicon Macs running macOS 26 are supported by the source.
- The supplied evidence does not confirm direct Docker Compose support, so Compose orchestration cannot be assumed.
- Equivalent handling for `seccomp`, `read_only`, `tmpfs`, PID limits, memory limits, healthchecks, and named volumes must be verified individually.
- Playwright browser execution and shared-memory requirements may behave differently inside the source’s VM-backed containers.
- Depending on an external system service adds installation and startup requirements for contributors.

## Acceptance criteria

- The target subsystem has a focused test.
- The integration preserves the target repository's existing behavior.
